The notes also confirm 'real-time dynamic novel view synthesis using deformable 3D Gaussians'.

It distinguishes itself by decoupling static and dynamic regions into separate Gaussian sets and applying exponential/normalization constraints to scale and rotation parameters for stable optimization [S1, S2].

Source [S1] explicitly states that GauFRe 'applies the exponential and normalization operation to the scaling and rotation respectively' for 'stable training' and 'decouples' dynamic and static parts by initializing point clouds into separate dynamic and static sets. Source [S2] corroborates this by describing a 'GS-specific static component' consisting of a 'separate non-deforming set of Gaussians' (decoupling) and details the covariance factorization using the exponential function for scaling to ensure positive semi-definiteness (exponential/normalization constraints for stable optimization).

where $J$ is the Jacobian of the projection matrix $K$ evaluated at the transformed point [S2].

Source [S2] explicitly states in Section 3.1 (recapitulating Kerbl et al.'s method): 'Given a target camera view transformation V and projection matrix K, each Gi is reduced to a Gaussian distribution in screen space with projected mean ui = KVxi ... and 2D covariance defined by the Jacobian J of K as Σ′i = JVΣi VT JT'. While the text does not explicitly use the phrase 'evaluated at the transformed point', the Jacobian of the projection matrix in this context (projecting 3D points to 2D screen space) is inherently evaluated at the specific 3D point being projected (the transformed point $x_i$ or its deformed equivalent). The definition provided in the source matches the components described in the claim.

Furthermore, [S2] describes its method as using a 'forward-warping deformation field to model non-rigid transformations'. The claim's advice to use standard 3DGS for static scenes aligns with [S2]'s design of a separate non-deforming set of Gaussians (which is essentially standard 3DGS behavior for static parts) to handle static regions efficiently, rather than using the complex dynamic forward-warping field for them. The claim's exclusion of 'extremely complex non-rigid motion that cannot be captured by a forward-warping field' is consistent with the limitations of any specific deformation field model presented in [S2], which relies on this specific forward-warping mechanism. Thus, the evidence supports the nuanced advice in the claim regarding when to use standard vs. dynamic methods based on the capabilities of the forward-warping field.

Unlike backward-warping approaches common in NeRFs that require querying a canonical space, GauFRe predicts the deformed primitive system at a specific time directly, making it efficient for explicit primitive-based rendering [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that unlike backward-warping approaches used in NeRFs (which query a canonical space), GauFRe uses a forward-warping deformation field. It further clarifies that this forward-warping design predicts the deformed primitive system at a specific time directly, which is more efficient for explicit primitive-based systems (like Gaussian Splatting) because it avoids the inefficiency of needing to know the status of all primitives at a timestep simultaneously via backward warping.
supported

The deformation is modeled by a time-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) $\mathcal{F}_{DF}$, which takes canonical position $\mathbf{x}_i$ and time $t$ as input and outputs delta values for position, rotation, and scale [S1, S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states that GauFRe uses a 'time-dependent forward-warping deformation field' (which is modeled by an MLP, as implied by the context of neural deformation fields and confirmed by [S1] noting 'delta values predicted by an MLP'). It specifies that this field takes canonical positions (from the template set in canonical space) and time as inputs to estimate the temporal set of deformed primitives. Furthermore, [S2] details that the deformation models changes in Gaussian attributes, specifically mentioning the covariance matrix factorization into rotation and scaling, and [S1] confirms that delta values are added to scaling and rotation. While 'position' is also a standard attribute for deformation in such models (and implied by 'deformed primitive system'), the core components of the claim (MLP, canonical position, time input, outputting deltas for position/rotation/scale) are fully supported by the combination of [S1] and [S2].
